blocks.recap_md: Tree recursion is introduced through the direct recursive definition of the Fibonacci sequence, translated almost verbatim from Fib(n) = Fib(n-1) + Fib(n-2) into a Scheme procedure.

Tracing (fib 5) shows the computation branching into a tree (two calls per invocation), and this naive fib recomputes so much redundant work that its step count grows exponentially with n even though the space it needs grows only linearly.
An alternative linear-iteration formulation of Fibonacci is derived, carrying a running pair (a, b) forward through simultaneous updates instead of branching into subcalls.

The text argues tree recursion isn't useless despite the inefficiency, notes that finding the iterative Fibonacci algorithm took real cleverness, and then poses the classic change-making problem: counting the ways to make change for a given amount using a set of coin denominations.

A recursive relation for counting ways to make change is worked out: splitting into 'ways without the first coin kind' plus 'ways using the reduced amount with all coin kinds', justified by dividing all ways to make change into those two disjoint groups.
Degenerate base cases (zero amount, negative amount, no coin kinds left) are specified, and the whole reduction is translated into the count-change/cc/first-denomination Scheme procedures.

Running (count-change 100) with the five standard US coin denominations returns 292, but this count-change process is tree-recursive with the same kind of redundancy as naive fib, prompting the idea of a hypothetical 'smart compiler' that could turn such easy-to-write-but-inefficient procedures into efficient ones automatically.

The section closes with three exercises: defining a three-term recursive/iterative function f, writing a recursive procedure for entries of Pascal's triangle, and proving the closed-form golden-ratio formula for Fib(n).

knowledge_items.statement: Tree recursion is exemplified by the naive recursive Fibonacci procedure, translated directly from its two-case mathematical definition: evaluating (fib n) (for n > 1) triggers two further recursive calls, so the shape of the resulting computation is a tree that branches into two at every level except at the base cases.

The naive tree-recursive fib procedure does a huge amount of redundant computation (whole subtrees get recomputed many times), so its number of steps grows exponentially with n, even though the space it needs grows only linearly with n (proportional to the tree's maximum depth rather than its number of nodes) - in sharp contrast to the linear-step, constant-space iterative fib-iter formulation of the same function.

The counting-change problem (how many ways to make change for a given amount using given coin denominations) is a second natural example of tree recursion: the number of ways to change amount a with n kinds of coins reduces to (ways not using the first kind of coin) plus (ways to change the reduced amount a-d using all n kinds), and evaluating it produces a similarly redundant, tree-shaped computation.

Tree-recursive processes, though often far less efficient than an iterative equivalent, can be considerably easier to derive and understand: the direct fib procedure is little more than a transcription of the Fibonacci definition, while finding the linear fib-iter took extra cleverness, and no comparably obvious efficient algorithm for count-change is given either.

questions.prompt: Why does the process generated by evaluating (fib 5) with the direct recursive definition trace out a tree shape rather than a straight line of calls?
options: Because each invocation of fib (except the base cases n=0 and n=1) makes two recursive calls, so the tree of calls branches into two at every level
Because Scheme automatically parallelizes recursive calls into separate branches for performance
Because fib recomputes (fib 0) and (fib 1) only once each, and the tree is just a visual artifact of caching those results
Because the cond special form forces every clause's branch to be evaluated regardless of which one actually matches
questions.explanation: fib calls itself twice per non-base invocation (once for n-1 and once for n-2), and this branching-in-two repeats at every level of the recursion, which is exactly what produces the tree-shaped evolved process.

questions.prompt: What is the actual growth-rate tradeoff of the naive tree-recursive fib procedure, compared to the linear iterative fib-iter version?
options: The tree-recursive version needs a number of steps that grows exponentially with n but only linear space (proportional to tree depth); the iterative version needs only linear steps and constant space
Both versions need the same number of steps, but the tree-recursive version uses less memory because it never keeps prior results around
The tree-recursive version needs linear steps but exponential space, since it must store every subtree it ever computes
The tree-recursive version is actually faster in practice, because modern Scheme compilers automatically eliminate its redundant subtree computations
questions.explanation: The number of steps for the tree-recursive process is proportional to the number of nodes in the tree, which grows exponentially (roughly like Fib(n) itself); the space needed is only proportional to the tree's maximum depth, i.e. linear in n - unlike the iterative version's linear steps and constant space.

questions.prompt: According to the reduction rule given for count-change, the number of ways to change amount a using n kinds of coins equals what?
options: The number of ways to change a using all but the first kind of coin, plus the number of ways to change (a - d) using all n kinds of coins, where d is the first kind's denomination
The number of ways to change a using only the first kind of coin, plus the number of ways to change a using only the remaining n-1 kinds
The number of ways to change a using n-1 kinds of coins, multiplied by the number of coin kinds available
The number of ways to change a/n using each single kind of coin, summed over all n kinds
questions.explanation: The relation splits all ways of making change into two disjoint groups: those that never use the first kind of coin (leaving n-1 kinds to change the same amount a), and those that use at least one of the first kind of coin (which reduces to changing the smaller amount a-d with all n kinds still available).

questions.prompt: What does the text conclude, using the fib and count-change examples, about the relationship between how easy a process is to derive and how efficient it turns out to be?
options: A tree-recursive formulation can be far easier to come up with and understand than an efficient iterative equivalent, even though it may be much less efficient - devising the linear fib-iter took extra cleverness, and no comparably simple efficient algorithm for count-change was obvious either
Tree-recursive processes are always both easier to derive and more efficient than any iterative alternative, so iteration is only useful for simple numerical loops
Any tree-recursive procedure can be mechanically turned into an equally efficient iterative one just by reordering its cond clauses
Ease of derivation and runtime efficiency are unrelated properties that the text says have no connection to each other in general
questions.explanation: The direct fib procedure is presented as little more than a transcription of the mathematical definition, while arriving at fib-iter required noticing a less obvious reformulation with extra state variables; similarly, no comparably simple efficient count-change algorithm is given, illustrating that easy-to-derive and efficient are not the same thing.
